newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian confesses to Port Arthur massacre.
newsitem.headline: Australian confesses to Port Arthur massacre.

text.p: Martin Bryant, accused of the worst mass killing in modern Australian history, laughed on Thursday as he confessed to all 35 murders at the Port Arthur tourist site in April, reversing earlier pleas of not guilty.

Making an unexpected court appearance here in the island state of Tasmania, Bryant used a routine pre-trial hearing to change his pleas, at times breaking into laughter or putting his hand to his mouth to stifle a grin as the charges were read.

Bryant, 29, wearing a pale blue suit and unkept collar-length blond hair, wore a smile as he entered the dock, then occasionally broke into a grin as he eyeballed weeping relatives of victims and massacre survivors seated close by.

As each of a total of 72 charges were read out in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, Bryant either leaned into a microphone and mumbled "guilty" or gazed around the room as he admitted his guilt in a loud, clear voice.

He took frequent sips of water and once almost overbalanced as he pulled his head back with mute laughter after pleading guilty to murdering the massacre's youngest victim, three-year-old girl Madeline Mikac.

Australia's worst modern day massacre began on a peaceful Sunday afternoon on April 28 when Bryant opened fire on tourists with a high-powered rifle among the stone ruins of a former penal colony at Port Arthur, on Tasmania's southeast coast.
Within minutes 24 people were dead, some where they sat eating their lunch. Within an hour the death toll was 32 and by sunrise the next day 35 people were dead.

Bryant was arrested the next morning as he fled a nearby burning guesthouse where the last three victims were found. He suffered burns and was taken to hospital but was later transferred to a maximum security jail after death threats.
On September 30, Bryant appeared in court and pleaded not guilty to all charges and was due to stand trial on November 19.
But on Thursday, he shocked Australia by confessing to all 72 charges, including 20 counts of attempted murder, in a court appearance that took just 30 minutes.
Judge William Cox adjourned the case until November 19 for a plea of mitigation and sentencing.
Bryant's lawyer, John Avery, later declined to explain why Bryant had reversed his pleas.
"All I can say is we have been doing a lot of talking over the past few weeks and I am gratified that the right decision has been made," Avery told reporters.
"I hope it makes a real difference and hope it allays people's concerns as to the trauma of having a trial," he added.

Over 100 witnesses were to have been called for a full trial, though some survivors still deeply traumatised by the killings were crossed off the prosecution's witness list at the request of counsellors, a social worker told Reuters.
Prosecutor Damian Bugg said he was relieved he no longer needed to put grieving people in the witness box.
"Faced with the task of calling so many people to give evidence in a trial, I am relieved for their sake and for the community's sake," Bugg told reporters.
But he said the prosecution still needed to question people in order to prepare a submission to the mitigation hearing and sentencing.
Some relatives and friends of Port Arthur victims left the court holding hands. A Tasmanian state government spokesman asked the media throng to respect their privacy.
"They have lost wives and children...and they are looking for an end to it," spokesman Peter Hazelwood said.
Judge Cox warned the media against prejudicing Bryant's hearing on November 19 and said publication of prejudicial material would "commit a grave contempt of this court".
"The accused must be afforded full opportunity to place before me all facts and circumstances relevant to a plea of mitigation," Cox said.
